issues.legal_issue: A High Court must follow a Supreme Court declaration of law that applies to the relevant issue, even where an earlier High Court decision conflicts with that declaration.
material_facts: The Supreme Court had previously applied its interpretation of a rent-law exclusion to the corresponding exclusion in the state rent law.
That application conflicted with an earlier High Court decision concerning the state-law exclusion.
The High Court relied on the earlier High Court decision and directed the parties to pursue eviction remedies before the rent court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was bound by the Supreme Court’s declaration and could not prefer or distinguish the conflicting High Court decision; the earlier High Court decision stood impliedly overruled to the extent of the conflict.
issues.legal_principle: Article 141 makes law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India. The Court relied on its prior decision in Shobha Surendar, which applied D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India to Section 31 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act; Padmanabha Rao v. State of Karnataka was impliedly overruled to the extent that it was inconsistent. The Court also referred to Rattan Arya v. State of Tamil Nadu, but held that the High Court could not use it to depart from the Supreme Court’s declaration.

predicates.high_court_case: The matter is before a High Court.
predicates.supreme_court_declaration_applies: The Supreme Court has declared law that applies to the issue before the High Court.
predicates.high_court_relies_on_conflicting_precede: The High Court relies on a precedent that conflicts with the applicable Supreme Court declaration.
predicates.high_court_must_follow_supreme_court_dec: The High Court is required to follow the applicable Supreme Court declaration.

issues.definition: When a matter is before a High Court, an applicable Supreme Court declaration controls over conflicting precedent on which the High Court might otherwise rely.

issues.legal_issue: A civil eviction suit may proceed for premises excluded from rent-control protection by the applicable rent-law exclusion.
material_facts: The landlord brought a civil suit seeking possession of commercial premises and relied on an exclusion from rent-control protection for premises above a specified monthly rent.
The Supreme Court’s applicable declaration treated the state-law exclusion as operative, contrary to the High Court’s direction that the parties pursue eviction before the rent court.
The trial court had decreed eviction, and the Supreme Court restored that decree after setting aside the High Court’s order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to direct the parties to seek their remedies under the Rent Control Act, and the trial court’s eviction decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 31 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act excluded premises above the specified rent from the Act. The Court applied D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India, concerning a similar exclusion under the Delhi Rent Control Act, as applied to the Karnataka provision in Shobha Surendar. It therefore rejected the High Court’s reliance on Padmanabha Rao and restored the civil court’s decree. Section 21 was relevant to eviction under the Rent Control Act, but did not govern premises excluded from that Act.

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord has brought a civil suit seeking eviction or possession of premises.
predicates.premises_excluded_from_rent_control: The premises fall outside rent-control protection under an applicable exclusion.
predicates.landlord_seeks_possession: The landlord seeks possession of the premises from the occupant.
predicates.civil_court_may_adjudicate_eviction: The civil court may hear and decide the eviction claim.

issues.definition: A civil court may decide a landlord’s eviction claim when the suit seeks possession of premises that are excluded from rent-control protection.

issues.legal_issue: The continued operation of a rent-law exclusion is not invalid merely because it leaves many premises outside the statute’s protection as rents and circumstances change.
material_facts: The respondents argued that prevailing commercial rents meant the exclusion would place many premises outside the rent law’s protection.
The rent law had been extended over time, and the Court considered that the legislature would have been aware of prevailing rents.
The Court considered that the legislature might have chosen to reserve statutory protection for tenants paying lower rents.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the argument that the exclusion should be treated as invalid on that basis, observing that any change in policy was for the legislature to make.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered Malpe Vishwanath Acharya v. State of Maharashtra, Rattan Arya v. State of Tamil Nadu, Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Sant Lal Bharti v. State of Punjab, which were cited on the possibility that changed circumstances may affect a law’s validity. It relied on the approach in D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India that a legislature may limit rent-control protection according to its policy, and stated that any policy change was for the legislature.

predicates.challenge_to_rent_law_exclusion: A party challenges the validity of an exclusion from rent-law protection.
predicates.legislature_aware_of_prevailing_rents: The legislature enacted or continued the law with awareness of prevailing rents.
predicates.protection_limited_by_rent_level: The law limits protection according to the rent payable for the premises.
predicates.exclusion_not_invalidated_on_that_basis: The exclusion is not invalidated solely because it leaves many premises outside the law’s protection in light of prevailing rents or changed circumstances.

issues.definition: When a rent-law exclusion reflects a legislatively chosen rent-based limit adopted with awareness of prevailing rents, the exclusion is not invalidated solely because many premises fall outside the law’s protection.
